title: How to Use a Spurtle for Sourdough Baguettes Mixing
meta_description: Master the art of mixing sourdough baguettes with a wooden spurtle. Learn step‑by‑step techniques, tips, and how the 2‑piece spurtle set makes dough handling ef
html:
When you’re mixing sourdough baguettes, the tool you choose can spell the difference between a smooth, elastic dough and a stubborn, over‑worked mess. A wooden spurtle—especially the 2 PCS Wooden Spurtle Spatula for Sourdough Starter, Wood Danish Dough Whisk—offers a low‑profile, non‑scratch surface that lets you blend starter, flour, water, and salt with precision. Below is a practical, hands‑on guide that walks you through every stage of baguette mixing, from starter integration to final dough development.

Why a Spurtle Beats a Traditional Spoon or Whisk for Mixing Sourdough Baguettes

Traditional metal whisks create a lot of turbulence, which can tear the gluten network before it has a chance to form. A spurtle’s slender, flat blade moves dough in a gentle, circular motion, encouraging the gluten strands to line up rather than snap. The wooden construction also stays cool, preventing premature heat transfer that can accelerate fermentation unevenly.

Preparing Your Levain: The First Mix

Before you even think about the baguette dough, you need a healthy starter. Using the Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set, follow these steps:

  1. Measure 50 g of active starter and 50 g of whole‑grain flour into a clean glass jar.
  2. Add 50 g of lukewarm water.
  3. Insert the skinny wooden spurtle spatula and stir clockwise until the mixture is uniform. The spurtle’s tapered tip helps scrape the jar’s sides, ensuring no dry flour pockets remain.
  4. Cover the jar and let it sit at room temperature for 4‑6 hours, or until it doubles in volume.

Because the spurtle is non‑scratch, you can reuse the same jar for multiple feedings without worrying about lingering residues.

Autolyse: Letting Flour Hydrate Before Mixing Sourdough Baguettes

Once your levain is ready, combine the main dough ingredients. Autolyse (mixing flour and water only) improves extensibility and reduces mixing time. Here’s how to do it with your spurtle:

  • Weigh 500 g of bread flour and 350 g of water into a large mixing bowl.
  • Using the Danish‑style dough stick, fold the flour into the water a few times until no dry spots remain. The spurtle’s thin edge penetrates the mass without tearing it.
  • Let the mixture rest for 30‑45 minutes. During this period the flour fully hydrates, and gluten begins to develop naturally.

When the autolyse is complete, you’ll notice a slightly sticky but cohesive mass—exactly what you want before adding the levain.

Incorporating Levain and Salt: Mixing Sourdough Baguettes Properly

Now it’s time to bring everything together. The spurtle shines here because you can fold the levain into the autolysed dough without over‑mixing.

1. Add the risen levain (about 150 g) and 10 g of sea salt to the bowl.
2. Using the wooden spurtle, perform a series of stretch‑and‑fold motions: lift the dough from the side, stretch it upward, and fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl and repeat until the dough feels smooth and slightly tacky, usually 4–6 minutes.

Because the spurtle’s surface is smooth, you’ll avoid any tiny scratches that could harbor bacteria—a subtle advantage when dealing with a long‑fermenting sourdough culture.

Bulk Fermentation and Folding: Keeping the Dough Light

After the initial mix, let the dough rest for 30 minutes, then perform a series of folds every 30‑45 minutes during the 3‑4 hour bulk fermentation. Each fold is executed with the same spurtle you used earlier:

  1. Wet the spurtle lightly to prevent sticking.
  2. Lift one edge of the dough, stretch it upward, and fold it back onto itself.
  3. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat until you’ve completed four folds.

This gentle handling maintains the dough’s airy structure, which is crucial for that classic baguette crumb.

Shaping, Scoring, and Baking: The Final Steps

When the dough has doubled in size and shows visible bubbles, turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Use the skinny wooden spurtle to scrape any excess flour from the work surface—its narrow profile lets you get into corners without damaging your countertop.

Divide the dough into three equal pieces, pre‑shape them into rounds, let them rest 20 minutes, then shape each into a baguette. Place the loaves on a parchment‑lined baking sheet, slash the tops with a lame, and bake at 475°F (245°C) with steam for the first 15 minutes. The result is a crisp, caramelized crust and an open, irregular crumb that only true sourdough can deliver.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Wooden Spurtle

After you’ve finished baking, rinse the spurtle with warm water and a soft brush—no soap is needed unless you’ve used a lot of butter. Dry it immediately to prevent warping. Occasionally rub the wood with a food‑grade mineral oil to keep it from drying out. Because the spurtle is non‑scratch, you can use it on stainless steel bowls, glass jars, and even silicone mats without worrying about surface damage.

FAQ

Can I use a metal whisk instead of a spurtle for mixing sourdough baguettes?

Yes, but a metal whisk creates more turbulence and can over‑work the gluten early in the process. A spurtle provides a gentler, more controlled mix, which yields a better crumb and easier handling.

Is the wooden spurtle safe for use with acidic sourdough starter?

Absolutely. The wood is naturally resistant to mild acidity, and because you don’t soak it in water for long periods, it won’t absorb the starter’s acids in a way that affects flavor.

How often should I oil my wooden spurtle?

Apply a thin layer of food‑grade mineral oil once a month, or whenever the wood starts to look dry. This keeps the spurtle smooth, prevents cracking, and extends its life.
